Graphene oxide was chemically prepared by improved Hummer’s method.
Single-step reduction methods included hydrazine hydrate chemical reduction and thermal annealing at 800°C in argon/hydrogen atmosphere.
Double-step reduction methods combined hydrazine hydrate reduction with either 50 keV nitrogen ion beam implantation or 100 MeV silver ion swift heavy ion irradiation.
Raman spectroscopy showed an increase in I(D)/I(G) ratio from 0.92 in GO to 1.58 in sample S, indicating increased defects and smaller sp2 domains after reduction.
FT-IR spectra confirmed removal of epoxy groups in hydrazine hydrate reduced samples but not in thermally annealed samples.
SEM images revealed aggregated sheet structures that opened up after reduction.
Carbon to oxygen atomic ratio increased from 1.21 in GO to 14.5 in sample S, confirming reduction.
Room temperature dc electrical conductivity increased from 2.25 x 10^-9 S/cm in GO to 235.03 S/cm in sample S.
EMI shielding effectiveness (SE) at 12.4 GHz increased from 31.14 dB in sample C to 55.29 dB in sample S.
Skin depth decreased with increasing electrical conductivity, with sample S having the lowest skin depth of 0.0188 cm.
Shielding effectiveness slightly increased with frequency within the X-band range.
Sample S's EMI shielding effectiveness surpasses many previously reported reduced graphene oxide composites.
Hydrazine hydrate reduction converts epoxy groups into hydrazine alcohols, facilitating removal of oxygen functionalities.
Thermal annealing cannot remove epoxy groups due to their stability up to 1200°C.
EMI shielding effectiveness is mainly due to reflection and absorption of electromagnetic waves; multiple reflections are negligible when SE > 10 dB.
The study demonstrates that combining chemical and ion beam reduction methods enhances electrical conductivity and EMI shielding performance.
The samples were prepared as rectangular pellets of 15.8 x 7.9 mm^2 and 0.9 mm thickness for EMI testing.
The highest EMI shielding effectiveness of 55.29 dB corresponds to over 99.999% attenuation of electromagnetic waves.
The study highlights reduced graphene oxide as a lightweight, non-corrosive alternative to metal-based EMI shields.
